React Components

React components are the basic building blocks of React applications. They allow developers to break large user interfaces into smaller, independent, and reusable pieces. Components are similar to JavaScript functions, but they are specially designed to return and manage UI elements.

In short, a React component is a block of code (written as a function or a class) that defines how a part of the user interface should look and behave.

Note: A React component is like a function that returns HTML elements.

Create Your First Component:

The name of a component must always start with a capital letter.

Example: 

function ReactFirstApp() {
  return (
    <h2>Hi, this is my first React app!</h2>
  );
}

Types of Components in React

There are two main types of React components:

  • Functional Components:

    These are JavaScript functions that accept data (called props) and return JSX. With the help of React Hooks, functional components can also manage state and lifecycle features, making them the most popular way of building modern React apps. 

    import React from 'react';

    function Greeting(props) {
      return <h1>Hello, {props.name}!</h1>;
    }

    export default Greeting;
  • Class Components:

    These are ES6 classes that extend React.Component. They use a render() method to return JSX and can also manage state and lifecycle methods. While still valid, class components are less common in new projects because functional components with Hooks are easier to use and maintain. 

    import React, { Component } from 'react';

    class GreetingClass extends Component {
      render() {
        return <h1>Hello, {this.props.name}!</h1>;
      }
    }

    export default GreetingClass;

Props in React Components

In React, "props" (short for properties) are a way to pass data from a parent component to a child component. They make components reusable and dynamic by allowing information to flow between components.

Note: Props are immutable (cannot be changed by the child component). They are used to communicate between components.

How to Use Props:

  • Passing Props: In the parent component, props are sent to the child component as attributes in JSX (just like HTML attributes). 

    function App() {
      return <ChildComponent name="Alice" age={30} />;
    }

  • Receiving Props: In the child component, props are received as an object. Functional components use props directly, while class components use this.props. 

    // Child Component (Functional)
    function ChildComponent(props) {
      return (
        <div>
          <p>Name: {props.name}</p>
          <p>Age: {props.age}</p>
        </div>
      );
    }

    // Child Component (Class)
    class ChildComponent extends React.Component {
      render() {
        return (
          <div>
            <p>Name: {this.props.name}</p>
            <p>Age: {this.props.age}</p>
          </div>
        );
      }
    }

React Functional Components

ReactJS functional components are plain JavaScript functions that accept props (properties) as an argument and return a React element, typically JSX, describing what should be rendered to the UI. They are the preferred way to write components in modern React development due to their simplicity and the introduction of Hooks.

Functional component with props

  • Functional components receive data from their parent components through props, which are read-only and should not be modified by the component itself. Props (short for “properties”).

    This allows components to be dynamic and reusable, as the data displayed can change based on what is passed in. 

    import React, { useState } from 'react';

    function Greeting(props) {
      const [name, setName] = useState(props.initialName || 'Guest');

      const handleChange = (event) => {
        setName(event.target.value);
      };

      return (
        <div>
          <h1>Hello, {name}!</h1>
          <input type='text' value={name} onChange={handleChange} />
        </div>
      );
    }

    export default Greeting;

In this example:

  • Greet is a functional component that accepts props.
  • useState is a Hook used to manage the name state within the component.
  • The component returns JSX, including an h1 tag and an input field.
  • The handleChange function updates the name state when the input value changes.

React Class Components

React class components are defined using ES6 classes and extend React.Component. They typically include the following structural elements: Import React.

Key Points

  • Must extend React.Component.
  • Has a render() method that returns JSX.
  • Can use state (stored inside this.state).
  • Props are accessed using this.props.
  • Supports lifecycle methods (e.g., componentDidMount).

Example: Simple Class Component

import React, { Component } from "react";

class Welcome extends Component {
  render() {
    return <h1>Hello, {this.props.name}!</h1>;
  }
}

export default Welcome;

Structure of React Class Components:

React class Component consist of following the parts

  • Class Declaration:

    A class component is defined as an ES6 class that extends React.Component. This inheritance provides access to React's component functionalities, such as state management and lifecycle methods.

    class Greet extends React.Component {
      // everything else goes inside this class
    }
  • Constructor:

    The constructor method is used for initializing the component's state and binding event handlers. It is called before the component is mounted. If a constructor is used, super(props) must be called as the first statement to correctly initialize the parent React.Component.

    class Greet extends React.Component {
      constructor(props) {
        super(props);
        this.state = { msg: "Hello Alice"}; // initializing state
      }
    }
  • Render Method:

    The render() method is the only mandatory method in a class component. It returns the JSX (JavaScript XML) that defines the component's UI. This method is called whenever the component needs to re-render, either due to state changes or prop updates.

    render() {
      return (
        <div>
          <h1>Hello, {this.props.name}</h1>
          <p>Count: {this.state.count}</p>
          <button onClick={this.handleClick}>Click Me</button>
        </div>
      );
    }
  • Props in Class Components:

    Props allow data to flow from parent components to child components. They are accessible via this.props. Props cannot be changed by the component itself; they are controlled by the parent component.

    class Greet extends React.Component {
      render() {
        return <h1>Hello, {this.props.name}</h1>;
      }
    }

React Hooks

React Hooks are functions introduced in React 16.8 that allow developers to use state and other React features in functional components without needing to write class components. They provide a more direct API to React concepts like state, lifecycle, and context within functional components, promoting a more functional programming style and improving code readability.

1. useState

This hook allows functional components to manage state. It returns an array containing the current state value and a function to update it.

Syntax: 

const [state, setState] = useState(initialValue);

  • state: The current state value.
  • setState: A function used to update the state.
  • initialValue: The initial state value.

2. useEffect

This hook is used to perform side effects in functional components, such as data fetching, subscriptions, or manually changing the DOM. It runs after every render by default, but its behavior can be controlled using a dependency array.

Syntax: 

useEffect(() => { effect }, [dependencies]);

  • effect: A function containing code that runs as a side effect (like API calls or DOM updates).
  • dependencies: An array of values that determines when the effect runs. Empty array [] means it runs once after the first render.

3. useContext

This hook allows functional components to subscribe to React context, making it easier to share values like themes or user authentication status across the component tree without prop drilling.

Syntax: 

const value = useContext(MyContext);

  • value: The current context value.
  • MyContext: The React context object created using React.createContext().

4. useReducer

An alternative to useState for managing more complex state logic, especially when state transitions depend on the previous state or involve multiple sub-values.

Syntax: 

const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(reducer, initialState);

  • state: The current state value.
  • dispatch: A function used to dispatch actions that will update the state.
  • reducer: A function that defines how the state should change based on the dispatched action.
  • initialState: The initial state value.

5. useRef

useRef is a React Hook that provides a way to create a mutable reference to a value that persists across component re-renders without causing the component to re-render when the value changes. It returns a plain JavaScript object with a single property called current.

Syntax: 

const ref = useRef(initialValue);

  • ref: A reference object that persists across renders.
  • initialValue: The initial value for the ref (usually null when referencing DOM elements).
  • Use ref.current to access or modify the value.
